prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

This article gives the proof of results announced in [J. Blanc, Finite Abelian subgroups of the Cremona group of the plane, C.R. Acad. Sci. Paris, S\'er. I 344 (2007), 21-26.] and some description of automorphisms of rational surfaces.   Given a finite Abelian subgroup of the Cremona group of the plane, we provide a way to decide whether it is birationally conjugate to a group of automorphisms of a minimal surface.   In particular, we prove that a finite cyclic group of birational transformations of the plane is linearisable if and only if none of its non-trivial elements fix a curve of positive genus. For finite Abelian groups, there exists only one surprising exception, a group isomorphic to Z/2ZxZ/4Z, whose non-trivial elements do not fix a curve of positive genus but which is not conjugate to a group of automorphisms of a minimal rational surface.   We also give some descriptions of automorphisms (not necessarily of finite order) of del Pezzo surfaces and conic bundles.

outputs.L2:
This paper supplies the proofs of the results previously announced in [J. Blanc, *Finite Abelian subgroups of the Cremona group of the plane*, C.R. Acad. Sci. Paris, Sér. I 344 (2007), 21–26], together with certain descriptions of automorphisms of rational surfaces.  

For any finite Abelian subgroup of the plane Cremona group, we present a criterion for determining whether it is birationally conjugate to a group acting by automorphisms on a minimal surface. In particular, we show that a finite cyclic group of birational self-maps of the plane can be transformed into a linear group exactly when no non-identity element of the group leaves invariant a curve of positive genus.  

In the Abelian finite case, there is a single exceptional phenomenon: a group isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}\). Although none of its non-trivial elements fixes a positive-genus curve, it is nevertheless not conjugate to an automorphism group of any minimal rational surface.  

We also include descriptions of automorphisms, not necessarily of finite order, of del Pezzo surfaces and conic bundles.
outputs.L3:
The article establishes in full detail several results that had previously been announced by J. Blanc concerning finite Abelian subgroups of the plane Cremona group, the group of birational transformations of the projective plane. Its main purpose is to clarify when such groups can be understood, up to birational conjugacy, as groups of automorphisms of rational surfaces, and in particular of minimal rational surfaces.

A central contribution of the article is a practical method for determining whether a finite Abelian subgroup of the Cremona group is birationally conjugate to a group of automorphisms of a minimal surface. This gives a systematic way to pass from an abstract finite Abelian group of birational transformations to a more geometric model, where the group acts regularly on a rational surface such as a del Pezzo surface or a conic bundle. In this setting, “minimal” means that the surface admits no further equivariant birational contraction compatible with the group action.

One of the principal results concerns finite cyclic subgroups of the Cremona group. The article proves that such a group is linearisable—that is, birationally conjugate to a subgroup of the automorphism group of the projective plane—if and only if none of its non-trivial elements fixes a curve of positive genus. Thus, for cyclic groups, the existence of a fixed curve of positive genus is precisely the obstruction to linearisability.

The article also shows that the analogous criterion for more general finite Abelian groups has a single exceptional case. There exists one exceptional finite Abelian group, isomorphic to  
\[
\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z},
\]
which is not birationally conjugate to a group of automorphisms of a minimal rational surface, even though none of its non-trivial elements fixes a curve of positive genus. This group therefore represents the unique obstruction to extending the cyclic linearisability criterion directly to all finite Abelian subgroups.

In addition to these classification and conjugacy results, the article describes various automorphisms of del Pezzo surfaces and conic bundles. The discussion includes both finite-order automorphisms and certain automorphisms of infinite order, thereby giving a broader picture of how Abelian groups can act on the main classes of rational surfaces that arise in the study of the Cremona group.

The article investigates finite Abelian subgroups of the plane Cremona group, that is, the group of birational transformations of the projective plane. Its main purpose is to understand when such groups can be simplified, up to birational conjugacy, into groups acting by biregular automorphisms on suitable rational surfaces. In particular, the paper studies the relationship between finite Abelian subgroups of the Cremona group and automorphism groups of minimal rational surfaces, such as del Pezzo surfaces and conic bundles.

A central theme of the article is the classification of these groups according to their birational behaviour. The author gives criteria for deciding whether a given finite Abelian subgroup of the Cremona group is birationally conjugate to a group of automorphisms of a minimal surface. This involves analyzing the fixed curves of elements of the group, especially curves of positive genus, since such curves provide important birational invariants.

One of the main results concerns finite cyclic subgroups. The article proves that a finite cyclic subgroup of the plane Cremona group is linearisable—that is, birationally conjugate to a subgroup of the automorphism group of the projective plane—if and only if no non-trivial element of the group fixes a curve of positive genus. Thus, the presence of a fixed curve of positive genus is precisely the obstruction to linearisation in the cyclic case.

The article also identifies a unique exceptional case among finite Abelian groups. Besides the expected linearisable groups, there exists a special Abelian group isomorphic to  
\[
\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z},
\]
which is not linearisable but has the property that none of its non-trivial elements fixes a curve of positive genus. This group therefore shows that the cyclic criterion does not extend directly to all finite Abelian subgroups.

In addition, the paper clarifies the structure of finite Abelian automorphism groups acting on rational surfaces. It gives a detailed analysis of their possible actions on del Pezzo surfaces and on conic bundles, describing when such actions are minimal and how they fit into the birational classification. Through this study, the article refines the understanding of how finite Abelian subgroups of the Cremona group arise and how they can be distinguished up to birational conjugacy.

Overall, the work provides a precise classification framework for finite Abelian subgroups of the plane Cremona group. It establishes a sharp linearisation criterion for cyclic groups, isolates the exceptional group \(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}\), and explains the role of del Pezzo surfaces and conic bundles in the birational geometry of rational surface automorphisms.

This is a reflection on the quiet beauty of limits. In a world that often feels endless, every moment is finite, shaped by time, choice, and memory. Like a sheet of pure blanc paper, life begins with space for meaning, waiting for words, colors, and experiences to fill it.

The finite nature of things does not make them less valuable. Instead, it gives them importance. A conversation matters because it cannot last forever. A day feels precious because it fades into evening. Even silence, clean and open like blanc, carries a kind of depth when we understand that it too will pass.

This is why limits can inspire us. They remind us to create, to notice, and to care. What is finite can still be beautiful, complete, and unforgettable.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write the abstract for a math research paper proving the results announced in Blanc’s 2007 C.R. Acad. Sci. note on finite Abelian subgroups of the plane Cremona group.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract.**  
We give a complete proof of the classification announced by Blanc in his 2007 note in *C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris* of finite Abelian subgroups of the plane Cremona group  
\[
\operatorname{Bir}(\mathbb P^2_{\mathbb C}).
\]
Using the equivariant minimal model program, every such group is realized as a group of automorphisms of a rational surface whose action is minimal, and hence the problem is reduced to the study of Abelian automorphism groups of del Pezzo surfaces and conic bundles. We determine all possibilities, describe explicit models and generators, and give the corresponding conjugacy criteria inside the Cremona group. In particular, we identify the linearizable groups, the de Jonquières-type groups, and the exceptional Abelian groups arising from low-degree del Pezzo surfaces. The resulting list is complete up to birational conjugacy and recovers, as special cases, the known classifications of cyclic subgroups of prime order and of elementary Abelian subgroups.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a paper about finite Abelian subgroups of the Cremona group of the plane, linearisability of cyclic birational transformations, and automorphisms of rational surfaces.
counterfactuals.output:
The paper studies **finite Abelian subgroups of the plane Cremona group**  
\[
\operatorname{Bir}(\mathbb P^2),
\]
the group of birational transformations of the complex projective plane. Its main goal is to understand when such groups are birationally conjugate to groups of projective linear automorphisms and to classify the genuinely non-linear examples.

## Main themes

### 1. Cremona group and rational surfaces

A central principle used in the paper is that finite subgroups of the Cremona group can be studied via their regular actions on smooth rational surfaces.

Given a finite subgroup  
\[
G \subset \operatorname{Bir}(\mathbb P^2),
\]
one can resolve indeterminacies and obtain a smooth rational surface \(S\) with a faithful biregular action of \(G\), together with a birational map
\[
S \dashrightarrow \mathbb P^2.
\]
Thus the problem becomes the classification of finite Abelian groups acting by automorphisms on rational surfaces, up to \(G\)-equivariant birational equivalence.

The paper uses the equivariant minimal model program for rational surfaces. A minimal pair \((S,G)\) is essentially of one of two types:

1. **Del Pezzo surfaces**, where \(-K_S\) is ample;
2. **Conic bundles**, rational surfaces equipped with a \(G\)-equivariant fibration over \(\mathbb P^1\) whose general fibre is a conic.

This dichotomy is the framework for the classification.

---

## 2. Linearisation problem

A key question is:

> When is a finite cyclic birational transformation of \(\mathbb P^2\) birationally conjugate to a linear automorphism of \(\mathbb P^2\)?

Equivalently, given an element
\[
g \in \operatorname{Bir}(\mathbb P^2)
\]
of finite order, when does there exist a birational map \(\varphi\) such that
\[
\varphi g \varphi^{-1} \in \operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb P^2)=\operatorname{PGL}_3(\mathbb C)?
\]

The paper shows that many finite cyclic transformations are linearisable, but there are important exceptions. These exceptions typically arise from automorphisms of special rational surfaces, especially del Pezzo surfaces or conic bundles, which cannot be equivariantly contracted to \(\mathbb P^2\).

A major result is a classification of **non-linearisable finite cyclic transformations**. The non-linear examples are closely related to automorphisms of:

- del Pezzo surfaces of small degree;
- conic bundles with special singular fibres;
- special involutions such as Bertini and Geiser involutions.

---

## 3. Finite Abelian subgroups

The paper goes beyond cyclic groups and classifies finite Abelian subgroups of the plane Cremona group up to birational conjugacy.

A basic source of examples comes from diagonal automorphisms of \(\mathbb P^2\):
\[
(x:y:z)\mapsto (\alpha x:\beta y:\gamma z),
\]
where \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) are roots of unity. These give finite Abelian subgroups of \(\operatorname{PGL}_3(\mathbb C)\), hence linearisable subgroups of the Cremona group.

However, not every finite Abelian subgroup is conjugate to a linear one. The paper identifies and classifies the non-linearisable possibilities.

The classification separates the groups according to the rational surface on which they act minimally:

### Del Pezzo case

If \(G\) acts minimally on a del Pezzo surface \(S\), then the degree
\[
K_S^2
\]
plays a crucial role.

For high-degree del Pezzo surfaces, the action is often birationally equivalent to a linear action on \(\mathbb P^2\). Non-linear phenomena occur mainly in low degree, especially degrees \(1,2,3,4\).

Important examples include:

- **Geiser involutions**, arising from del Pezzo surfaces of degree \(2\);
- **Bertini involutions**, arising from del Pezzo surfaces of degree \(1\);
- automorphisms of cubic surfaces;
- automorphisms of degree \(4\) del Pezzo surfaces.

These give finite Abelian subgroups of the Cremona group that are not conjugate to subgroups of \(\operatorname{PGL}_3(\mathbb C)\).

### Conic bundle case

If \(G\) preserves a conic bundle
\[
S \to \mathbb P^1,
\]
then the structure of \(G\) is constrained by its action on the base and on the fibres.

There is an exact sequence of the form
\[
1 \to G_F \to G \to G_B \to 1,
\]
where:

- \(G_F\) acts trivially on the base and fibrewise on the conics;
- \(G_B\) acts on the base \(\mathbb P^1\).

Since finite Abelian subgroups of \(\operatorname{PGL}_2(\mathbb C)\) are cyclic or isomorphic to \((\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^2\), this heavily restricts possible \(G_B\).

The paper classifies the possible Abelian groups preserving conic bundles and determines which are linearisable.

---

## 4. Main classification picture

The paper’s classification can be summarized as follows:

Every finite Abelian subgroup of the plane Cremona group is birationally conjugate to a group of automorphisms of a rational surface \(S\) where \((S,G)\) is minimal. Then:

1. If \(S\) is sufficiently simple, such as \(\mathbb P^2\) or \(\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1\), the group is linearisable or at least birationally equivalent to a standard automorphism group.

2. If \(S\) is a del Pezzo surface of low degree, genuinely new non-linear Abelian subgroups appear.

3. If \(S\) is a conic bundle with nontrivial singular fibres and a nontrivial fibrewise action, further non-linearisable Abelian groups occur.

Thus the finite Abelian subgroups of \(\operatorname{Bir}(\mathbb P^2)\) are described by reducing the problem to automorphism groups of minimal rational \(G\)-surfaces.

---

## 5. Cyclic groups and linearisability

One of the most concrete consequences concerns cyclic groups.

For an element of prime order \(p\), the paper gives a strong description of when it is linearisable. Roughly:

- Most cyclic transformations of prime order are linearisable.
- Non-linearisable examples occur only in special geometric situations.
- For large primes, the possibilities are extremely restricted.

In particular, the paper shows that if a cyclic birational transformation of prime order is not conjugate to a linear automorphism, then it must arise from a special automorphism of a rational surface, for example a del Pezzo surface or a conic bundle.

This gives a birational-geometric interpretation of the obstruction to linearisation.

---

## 6. Role of fixed curves

A recurring tool is the study of fixed curves.

If a finite-order birational transformation fixes a curve of positive genus, then that curve is a birational invariant of the conjugacy class. Linear automorphisms of \(\mathbb P^2\), by contrast, do not fix curves of positive genus pointwise.

Therefore, the presence of a fixed curve of genus \(>0\) is a powerful obstruction to linearisability.

Examples:

- A Geiser involution fixes a genus \(3\) curve.
- A Bertini involution fixes a genus \(4\) curve.
- Certain automorphisms of conic bundles fix hyperelliptic curves.

These fixed curves help distinguish non-linearisable Cremona transformations from linear ones.

---

## 7. Automorphisms of rational surfaces

The paper also contributes to the understanding of automorphism groups of rational surfaces.

It analyzes finite Abelian automorphism groups of:

- del Pezzo surfaces;
- conic bundles;
- blow-ups of \(\mathbb P^2\);
- surfaces with special configurations of exceptional curves.

The automorphism group is studied together with the action on the Picard group:
\[
\operatorname{Pic}(S).
\]
For a \(G\)-minimal surface, the invariant part
\[
\operatorname{Pic}(S)^G
\]
has small rank:

- rank \(1\) in the del Pezzo case;
- rank \(2\) in the conic bundle case.

This Picard-lattice viewpoint is essential for deciding whether equivariant contractions are possible and hence whether a group action is linearisable.

---

## 8. Overall contribution

The paper provides a classification of finite Abelian subgroups of the plane Cremona group and clarifies the linearisability problem for cyclic birational transformations.

Its main contributions are:

- reducing finite Abelian Cremona group actions to automorphisms of minimal rational surfaces;
- classifying the possible minimal pairs \((S,G)\);
- identifying which Abelian groups are birationally conjugate to linear groups;
- describing non-linearisable cyclic transformations;
- relating non-linearisability to fixed positive-genus curves and special rational surfaces;
- giving explicit geometric models for exceptional cases, such as Geiser and Bertini involutions and conic bundle automorphisms.

In short, the paper shows that finite Abelian subgroups of the plane Cremona group are largely controlled by the geometry of rational surfaces, and that the failure of linearisability is caused by a small number of special del Pezzo and conic bundle configurations.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a concise academic abstract mentioning criteria for when finite Abelian subgroups of the Cremona group are birationally conjugate to automorphism groups of minimal rational surfaces.
counterfactuals.output: We describe criteria for a finite Abelian subgroup \(G\) of the plane Cremona group \(\operatorname{Cr}_2(k)\) to be birationally conjugate to a subgroup of the automorphism group of a minimal rational surface. Using the \(G\)-equivariant minimal model program, such a subgroup is conjugate to \(\operatorname{Aut}(S)\) for a \(G\)-minimal rational surface \(S\) precisely when the induced action admits no \(G\)-equivariant birational contraction. Equivalently, the invariant Picard rank satisfies either \(\rho(S)^G=1\), in which case \(S\) is a del Pezzo surface, or \(\rho(S)^G=2\), in which case \(S\) carries a \(G\)-minimal conic-bundle structure. For Abelian groups, the possible minimal models are further constrained by the fixed-point structure, the action on the Picard lattice, and the preservation of exceptional curves or singular fibres. Thus birational conjugacy to automorphisms of minimal rational surfaces is characterized by the absence of invariant sets of disjoint \((-1)\)-curves and by compatibility of the Abelian action with either a del Pezzo polarization or a minimal conic fibration. These criteria provide a uniform framework for distinguishing linearizable Abelian subgroups from those whose Cremona conjugacy classes are represented only on nontrivial del Pezzo or conic-bundle models.
